values.label: Platelet count
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, under the heading “Platelets”: “Platelets are relatively small, 2–4 µ m in diameter, but numerous, with typically 150,000–160,000 per µ L of blood.”
values.note: OpenStax states this as a typical count (“typically”), so it is shown as given rather than widened; the saved text writes the unit as “µ L” (per microlitre).

states.label: Thrombocytopenia (too few platelets)
states.summary: Too few platelets circulate, so blood may not clot properly and excessive bleeding may result.

platelets.quote: If there is an insufficient number of platelets, called thrombocytopenia , blood may not clot properly, and excessive bleeding may result.
platelets.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, under the heading “Disorders of Platelets”

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, under the heading “Disorders of Platelets”: “If there is an insufficient number of platelets, called thrombocytopenia , blood may not clot properly, and excessive bleeding may result.” Also section 18.5 Hemostasis, under the heading “Disorders of Clotting”: “As discussed earlier, an insufficient number of platelets, called thrombocytopenia, typically results in the inability of blood to form clots.”
states.modelNote: The model lowers its platelet count, so the plug it builds is smaller.

states.label: Thrombocytosis (too many platelets)
states.summary: Too many platelets circulate, which may trigger unwanted blood clots (thrombosis).

platelets.quote: Thrombocytosis is a condition in which there are too many platelets. This may trigger formation of unwanted blood clots (thrombosis), a potentially fatal disorder.
platelets.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, under the heading “Disorders of Platelets”

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.4 Leukocytes and Platelets, under the heading “Disorders of Platelets”: “Thrombocytosis is a condition in which there are too many platelets. This may trigger formation of unwanted blood clots (thrombosis), a potentially fatal disorder.” Also section 18.5 Hemostasis, under the heading “Disorders of Clotting”: “In contrast to the disorders characterized by coagulation failure is thrombocytosis, also mentioned earlier, a condition characterized by excessive numbers of platelets that increases the risk for excessive clot formation, a condition known as thrombosis .”
states.modelNote: The model raises its platelet count, so the plug it builds is larger.

drugActions.label: Heparins
drugActions.summary: A short-acting anticoagulant that opposes prothrombin; a pharmaceutical form is given to people at risk of clots.

evidence.quote: And as noted earlier, basophils release heparin , a short-acting anticoagulant that also opposes prothrombin. Heparin is also found on the surfaces of cells lining the blood vessels. A pharmaceutical form of heparin is often administered therapeutically, for example, in surgical patients at risk for blood clots.
evidence.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.5 Hemostasis, under the heading “Plasma Anticoagulants”

drugActions.label: Vitamin K antagonists (warfarin)
drugActions.summary: Blocks the liver’s vitamin K step, so vitamin K–dependent clotting factors are made in a form that does not work.

evidence.quote: Other anticoagulant mechanisms include inhibition of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors by blocking hepatic γ-carboxylation, resulting in the production of functionally inactive factors with reduced calcium-binding capacity.
evidence.where: StatPearls, Anticoagulation Therapy (NBK560651), abstract, under the heading “Anticoagulation”

evidence.quote: Clotting factors are secreted primarily by the liver and the platelets. The liver requires the fat-soluble vitamin K to produce many of them.
evidence.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.5 Hemostasis, under the heading “Clotting Factors Involved in Coagulation”

drugActions.label: Factor Xa inhibitors
drugActions.summary: Block switched-on factor ten, which reduces thrombin generation and prevents fibrin clot formation.

evidence.quote: Direct thrombin inhibitors and direct factor Xa inhibitors reduce thrombin generation and prevent fibrin clot formation.
evidence.where: StatPearls, Anticoagulation Therapy (NBK560651), abstract, under the heading “Anticoagulation”

evidence.quote: Factor Xa converts prothrombin to thrombin as part of the prothrombinase complex, which includes factor V (cofactor), calcium, and platelet phospholipids.
evidence.where: StatPearls, Anticoagulation Therapy (NBK560651), abstract, under the heading “Coagulation Cascade”

drugActions.label: Direct thrombin inhibitors
drugActions.summary: Block thrombin itself, so fibrinogen is not turned into fibrin and the clot’s mesh does not form.

evidence.quote: Direct thrombin inhibitors and direct factor Xa inhibitors reduce thrombin generation and prevent fibrin clot formation.
evidence.where: StatPearls, Anticoagulation Therapy (NBK560651), abstract, under the heading “Anticoagulation”

evidence.quote: Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin and activates factor XIII, which cross-links fibrin to form a stable clot.
evidence.where: StatPearls, Anticoagulation Therapy (NBK560651), abstract, under the heading “Coagulation Cascade”

drugActions.label: Antiplatelet drugs
drugActions.summary: Stop platelets from clumping together (aggregation), through several different platelet signalling targets.

evidence.quote: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is very effective at inhibiting the aggregation of platelets.
evidence.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.5 Hemostasis, under the heading “Disorders of Clotting”

evidence.quote: Aspirin was the first antiplatelet medication and is a cyclooxygenase inhibitor.
evidence.where: StatPearls, Antiplatelet Medications (NBK537062), abstract (the indexed abstract has no section headings)

evidence.quote: The complexity of platelet signaling pathways provides multiple pharmacologic targets and underpins diverse antithrombotic therapies.
evidence.where: StatPearls, Physiology, Platelet (NBK470328), abstract (the indexed abstract has no section headings)

drugActions.label: Thrombolytics
drugActions.summary: Speed up the breakdown of an abnormal clot: tissue plasminogen activator turns plasminogen into plasmin, which breaks down fibrin.

evidence.quote: A class of drugs collectively known as thrombolytic agents can help speed up the degradation of an abnormal clot.
evidence.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.5 Hemostasis, under the heading “Disorders of Clotting”

evidence.quote: Tissue plasminogen activator is an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, the primary enzyme that breaks down clots.
evidence.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 18.5 Hemostasis, under the heading “Disorders of Clotting”

evidence.quote: Thrombolytic therapy plays a critical role in the rapid management of acute thromboembolic disorders by restoring blood flow, limiting ischemic tissue injury, and improving clinical outcomes.
evidence.where: StatPearls, Thrombolytic Therapy (NBK557411), abstract (the indexed abstract has no section headings)
